newsitem.title: UK: Britain's SFO enters fray in Co-op bid saga.
newsitem.headline: Britain's SFO enters fray in Co-op bid saga.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) on Tuesday added its weight to investigations surrounding Andrew Regan's failed bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).
The SFO told Reuters it had begun a probe into a controversial contract agreed in January 1995 between CWS and the Hobson Group. The SFO has not made any arrests in connection with the inquiry.

Regan was head of Hobson when in 1994, it bought the CWS food manufacturing group. A supply agreement between the two was extended in January 1995, after negotiations between Regan and two CWS managers.
Both the men, Allan Green and David Chambers, were dismissed by the supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group last weekend for their role in Regan's takeover attempt.
Regan, the 31-year-old behind the discredited 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) takeover plan, was not immediately available for comment.
He has been incommunicado since his Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica and its offshoot Galileo admitted defeat in the face of CWS legal action and the withdrawal of a key backer.
The SFO news was welcomed by the CWS, which said it would be co-operating fully with the investigation.
The takeover was scotched by a High Court injunction granted to the CWS preventing the use of confidential information leaked to Regan, his business associate David Lyons, Lanica and Galileo.
Green, the senior CWS executive who has admitted to passing on the highly sensitive papers, was sacked at the weekend following his suspension for a serious breach of trust only a week earlier.
Chambers, another CWS manager, was also sacked. The two men negotiated with Regan the extension of Hobson's supply agreement with CWS in 1995.
During the course of its bid defence, CWS raised doubts about a 2.4 million pound payment to a third party called Trellis International.
Regan has stated the money was paid by Hobson to Ronald Zimet at Trellis for "assisting with and conducting negotiations with CWS".

But the CWS was not happy with the answers it received from Regan and a week ago its lawyers Linklaters & Paine held a meeting with the SFO and passed on its concerns. The SFO decided on Monday to open the probe.
On Monday, Zimet resigned as non-executive chairman of British information services group Freepages.

SFO spokesman James O'Donoghue said the office, which investigates and prosecutes major financial frauds, was working in its investigation with the Greater Manchester police and the Metropolitan Police Fraud Squad.
He declined to comment on any operational aspects of the inquiry, including whether there had been any raids in connection with the probe or whether documents had been seized.
In an unrelated development, sources close to Galileo and Lanica confirmed that moves were underway for special bidding group Galileo to be put into voluntary liquidation.
"Its the right thing to do," said one source, adding it would return capital to shareholders.
Galileo is one of the parties named on the CWS High Court writ prohibiting the use of confidential information. It has also had costs awarded against it, along with Regan, Lyons, Green and Lanica.
Galileo was not immediately available for comment on its future plans. Its shareholders include stockbroker Killik & Co and fund managers Jupiter and Schroders Investment Management.
A Schroders spokesman declined to comment when asked about a newspaper report suggesting it was withdrawing from its business relationships with Lanica, Galileo and Regan.
On Monday, investment bank Hambros severed its ties with Regan and apologised unreservedly to CWS for its role in the takeover attempt, which first surfaced last February.
CWS also received an apology from law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite. Both settlements included "substantial" financial elements.
